newsitem.title: UK: West, Russia debate how to handle Serbia problem.
newsitem.headline: West, Russia debate how to handle Serbia problem.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

A month of protests in Serbia may now pose a real threat to President Slobodan Milosevic but Western governments are, for the most part, still treading carefully in their efforts to resolve the crisis.

One reason for the caution is that there is no clear successor to Milosevic and that he is regarded in some European capitals as a key player in making sure that the peace agreement for neighbouring Bosnia works properly.
Much is at stake, since NATO has just agreed to keep a peacekeeping force in Bosnia for another year, supporting continued international efforts to rebuild the country.

Diplomats and analysts say there are also different views between the United States, European allies and Russia on how far to back the opposition challenge which brought a record 250,000 people onto the streets of Belgrade at the weekend.

"There was a very cautious reaction when the protests first started and that has continued for many countries," said Michael Williams of the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) in London. "They worry about what comes after Milosevic."

At meetings this month, NATO foreign ministers and European Union leaders have joined in calling for the respect of democratic values and human rights in Serbia, warning Milosevic not to use violence in suppressing the protests.
But there are clear differences of emphasis.

The United States, which once relied heavily on Milosevic as a peacemaker in Bosnia, now seems prepared to go further than most others in calling for the president's socialist government to recognise the opposition's win in local elections last month.

U.S. envoy John Kornblum met Serbian opposition figures in Geneva on Sunday, a meeting which European diplomats say caused some concern elsewhere as it appeared to give direct blessing to their political aims.
Washington has also said it could consider imposing economic sanctions on Serbia, something others have not endorsed.

Russia -- which defended Serb interests throughout much of the recent Balkan conflict -- is at the other end of the scale, insisting that the crisis should be resolved internally and that there should be no outside interference.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Monday the international community should not apply pressure "to the point which would create inconveniences or serious difficulties for the peace process".

Among European allies, Britain and France are more cautious and believe that calling more or less openly for an end to Milosevic's rule is too risky and could provoke instability or even a bloody crackdown on protests.
Some diplomats say the collapse of Milosevic's rule could also renew pressures for more autonomy in areas of tension like Kosovo, populated largely by ethnic Albanians.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini called on the opposition to drop some of its demands during a visit to Belgrade last week and said afterwards that the international community was not seeking the removal of Milosevic.

British and French officials say they are working behind the scenes to convince Milosevic that he must change and broker a compromise with the opposition. They argue that these efforts are already showing results.

Courts in two Serbian towns have now handed victory in the local elections to the opposition Zajedno coalition, reversing earlier decisions, while an independent radio station is allowed to broadcast in Belgrade after being shut down briefly.

Milosevic has not used force to quell the protests, as he did in 1991, and has invited a team from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to examine last month's election results.

"We do not think it is right to get involved in the political fight and endorse one side or the other," said a diplomat from one of the more cautious European nations. "We may still have to live with Milosevic, after all."

However, Germany, Denmark and some others are closer to the U.S. view that Milosevic and the system he represents are clearly on the way out -- as happened with communism in Eastern Europe -- and that he should not be accommodated.

"The West faces a delicate task because it has to sort out the crisis without humiliating the Serbian president, all the while dealing with an opposition that might gain power," the French daily Le Figaro wrote on Monday.
